tiles.title: Inspect EC2 launch and health evidence

blocks.text: Launch choices include AMI, instance type and network placement. The AMI supplies the initial software image. Use the approved AMI, subnet and supplied instance profile; inspect the created ID and settings.
The profile attaches its IAM role; applications can use temporary role credentials. Read lifecycle state separately from reported host or instance health.

blocks.alt_text: Approved selections and created EC2 details; lifecycle state and status checks are separate panels.

blocks.text: The observed instance i-0c000000000000001 matches the approved AMI ami-0a000000000000001, type t3.micro and subnet subnet-0b000000000000001. The AMI is its initial software image. The supplied profile orders-sandbox-instance-profile attaches orders-sandbox-instance-role; applications can use that role’s temporary credentials.

Its lifecycle state is running, while the system check is ok and the instance check is impaired. Keep both kinds of evidence: running is not proof of health, and a completed launch does not replace status checks. The profile is a role container, not embedded application access keys.

steps.title: Distinguish state from health
steps.lede: Read the supplied evidence and choose the interpretation that keeps lifecycle and health separate.

blocks.text: Use approved launch choices, inspect the created identity and settings, and identify the role through its profile. Applications can use temporary role credentials. Record lifecycle state and status checks separately.

In the same EC2 evidence, state is running but the instance status check is impaired. State describes lifecycle; status checks report host or instance health. Retain both rather than treating running as proof of health.

remediation_steps.title: Reconnect launch choices and observed details

blocks.text: Launch choices include AMI, type and network placement; the AMI supplies the initial software image. Compare the created ID i-0c000000000000001 and settings with the approved AMI, subnet and supplied profile. The profile orders-sandbox-instance-profile attaches role orders-sandbox-instance-role; applications can use its temporary credentials. Contrast an approved request with observed instance evidence. Inspect state and status checks separately: running does not establish reported health.

An S3 object contains data and metadata; its key identifies it within a bucket. Upload with aws s3 cp from local file to bucket/key; download reverses the endpoints. Keep profile and Region explicit. Buckets are created in an AWS Region; verify location and caller access.

blocks.code:
aws s3 cp orders-release.zip s3://orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab/releases/orders-release.zip --profile orders-sandbox-operator --region us-east-1
aws s3 cp s3://orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab/releases/orders-release.zip retrieved/orders-release.zip --profile orders-sandbox-operator --region us-east-1

annotations.text: Upload: local → bucket/key; explicit profile and Region.
Download: same bucket/key → local; same explicit context.

steps.title: Verify the intended object and context

blocks.text: The upload goes from orders-release.zip to s3://orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab/releases/orders-release.zip. The download reads that same bucket/key into retrieved/orders-release.zip. The key releases/orders-release.zip identifies the object within orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab; a familiar local filename or key alone does not establish the intended storage location.

Both commands use profile orders-sandbox-operator and verified bucket Region us-east-1. The supplied access evidence says: Caller can upload and retrieve the intended bucket/key. After retrieval, the supplied comparison says: Retrieved artifact matches the supplied orders-release.zip file. A file arriving locally is not enough if its bucket/key differs from the intended object. Check endpoints, location and access rather than inferring them from the filename.

steps.title: Identify the object, then trace the transfer

blocks.text: An object contains data and metadata; identify it by bucket and key. Upload points from local to S3; download reverses the endpoints. Use explicit profile and Region, and verify bucket location and caller access.

blocks.title: Up next: Publish and select workload metrics
blocks.text: Next: match a workload metric’s complete identity.

In the same transfer evidence, upload has local source orders-release.zip and S3 destination s3://orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab/releases/orders-release.zip; download reverses the direction into a local destination. Use aws s3 cp with explicit profile orders-sandbox-operator and Region us-east-1 in both directions. A bucket is created in a Region: verify its intended location and caller access, rather than assuming them from the filename.

An S3 object consists of data and metadata. In the same evidence, releases/orders-release.zip is the key within bucket orders-sandbox-artifacts-lab; orders-release.zip is the local upload source. Those are different roles. With aws s3 cp, upload goes local → S3 bucket/key and download goes from that same S3 bucket/key → local, keeping explicit profile and Region. A familiar local filename is not a substitute for verifying the intended bucket/key.

A custom CloudWatch metric’s identity is namespace, name and dimension combination. Publish with put-metric-data, supplying namespace, name, value and intended dimensions. Distinct combinations identify distinct metrics; query the published combination to select the intended series.

right.alt_text: Two complete queries and one query omitting Service.

blocks.text: The sandbox publication is Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=sandbox, Service=orders, with supplied value 7. Publish using put-metric-data with that namespace, name, value and both dimensions. The staging publication is Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=staging, Service=orders, with supplied value 3. It is a distinct metric despite sharing the name.

The complete sandbox query selects Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=sandbox, Service=orders. A query omitting Service uses Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=sandbox: that is not the published sandbox orders combination. Compare the full published and queried identities, not only the metric name. These query records describe selections, not returned values; do not describe a staging series as the sandbox orders value.

steps.title: Check the selected series
steps.lede: Read the supplied identities and choose the query interpretation that matches the full published combination.

steps.title: Review metric publication excerpts
steps.lede: Read the supplied excerpts in this step and judge which publications specify the supplied namespace, metric name, value and intended dimensions.

blocks.text: Publish namespace, name, supplied value and intended dimensions with put-metric-data. A custom metric’s identity includes the complete dimension combination; query that same combination, not just a familiar name.

blocks.text: Continue to the next lesson.

A custom metric is identified by namespace, name and dimension combination. In the same evidence, Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=sandbox, Service=orders and Lab/Orders | QueueDepth | Environment=staging, Service=orders are distinct metrics. Query the complete published combination. Keeping Environment=sandbox but omitting Service=orders does not select the stated sandbox orders identity; matching the name alone is insufficient.

Use put-metric-data to publish the supplied namespace Lab/Orders, metric name QueueDepth, value 7 and dimensions Environment=sandbox, Service=orders. Contrast a complete publication with one missing an intended dimension. Namespace, name and the complete combination identify the metric; a different combination is a distinct metric. Query the same combination that was published.
